title: Calculus you will actually use
hook: Expanding gas pushes a piston with a pressure that keeps falling, so no single force times distance will do. How do you get the work it does from its pressure–volume diagram?
oneBreath: Calculus is the maths of things that change, and it has two halves that undo each other. The derivative is a rate, how fast one thing changes per unit of another at a single instant, like current as the rate charge flows; one rule finds the derivative of any power, and a slope of zero finds the largest or smallest value. The integral adds a rate up into a total, like charge from a current graph or work from a pV diagram, and the reverse of differentiating gets it exactly, right through to mean and RMS values.

ideas.title: Average rate of change
ideas.oneLine: Average rate between two points is the change in y divided by the change in x, the slope of the line joining them, with units.

ideas.title: The rate at an instant
ideas.oneLine: Slide two points together and the slope of the line joining them settles on one number: the rate at that instant, written dy/dx.

ideas.title: The derivative as a function
ideas.oneLine: Finding the rate at every point at once gives a new rule, the derivative f′(x), which for y = x² is 2x.

ideas.title: The power rule
ideas.oneLine: The derivative of xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹, worked term by term, so 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 gives 12x² − 4x + 7.

ideas.title: Rates on the job
ideas.oneLine: Read in its units, a derivative is a rate on the job: current is the rate charge flows, i = dq/dt, and velocity is displacement's.

ideas.title: Highest and lowest
ideas.oneLine: A smooth curve is flat where it turns at a top or bottom, so setting its derivative to zero finds the largest area or power.

ideas.title: Integration, the reverse
ideas.oneLine: Integrating undoes differentiating: xⁿ (n not −1) becomes xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1), plus a constant c fixed by a starting value.

ideas.title: Adding up: the definite integral
ideas.oneLine: Adding up bars under a rate graph gives the total, such as charge from current, and the reverse rule, F(b) − F(a), gets it exactly.

ideas.title: Work from a pV diagram
ideas.oneLine: The work a gas does is the area under its pV curve, which for pVⁿ = C is (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1).

ideas.title: Mean and RMS values
ideas.oneLine: Mean value is area ÷ length; RMS is the root of the squared graph's mean, which for a sine wave is its peak ÷ √2.

calibration.q: You drive 60 km out at 60 km/h, then the same 60 km back at 30 km/h. What was your average speed for the whole trip?
options: You cannot say without knowing your speed at every moment
calibration.why: The trip is 120 km and takes 1 hour out plus 2 hours back, so 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h. 45 km/h averages the two speeds, but you spend twice as long at 30. An average rate needs only the total change and the total time, not every moment.

calibration.q: A falling stone is doing 10 m/s at one exact instant. In that instant it moves no distance in no time. So what can the 10 m/s mean?
options: Nothing exact: a speed needs a stretch of time to mean anything
Its average speed over the whole fall so far
The distance it would cover each second if it carried on exactly as it is
calibration.why: It is the speed at that instant: 10 metres each second if nothing changed, the value averages over ever-shorter stretches close in on. It is exact, not meaningless. The average over the fall so far is lower, because the stone started from rest and has been speeding up.
